claim: Peripheral blood was collected from six healthy donors at three time points over the course of a year.
source: We collected peripheral blood from six healthy donors at three time points, where the second sample was collected 1 month after the first, and the third was collected 11 months after that (Figure 1A; Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the study design with six donors and three time points.

claim: Memory B cells were isolated using the markers CD19+ CD20+ CD27+.
source: These samples were subjected to fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to isolate memory B cells (Bmem: CD19+ CD20+ CD27+), plasmablasts (PBL: CD19low/+ CD20- CD27high CD138-), and plasma cells (PL: CD19low/+ CD20- CD27high CD138+; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the FACS markers used to isolate memory B cells.

claim: Plasmablasts were isolated using the markers CD19low/+ CD20- CD27high CD138-.
source: These samples were subjected to fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to isolate memory B cells (Bmem: CD19+ CD20+ CD27+), plasmablasts (PBL: CD19low/+ CD20- CD27high CD138-), and plasma cells (PL: CD19low/+ CD20- CD27high CD138+; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the FACS markers used to isolate plasmablasts.

claim: Plasma cells were isolated using the markers CD19low/+ CD20- CD27high CD138+.
source: These samples were subjected to fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to isolate memory B cells (Bmem: CD19+ CD20+ CD27+), plasmablasts (PBL: CD19low/+ CD20- CD27high CD138-), and plasma cells (PL: CD19low/+ CD20- CD27high CD138+; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the FACS markers used to isolate plasma cells.

claim: A total of 1.06×10^7 unique IGH cDNA molecules were obtained from 83 cell samples.
source: From a total of 83 cell samples, we obtained 1.06×107 unique IGH cDNA molecules, each covered by at least three sequencing reads, representing 8.4×105 unique IGH clonotypes (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides sequencing statistics from the study.

claim: The obtained IGH cDNA molecules represented 8.4×10^5 unique IGH clonotypes.
source: From a total of 83 cell samples, we obtained 1.06×107 unique IGH cDNA molecules, each covered by at least three sequencing reads, representing 8.4×105 unique IGH clonotypes (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides sequencing statistics from the study.

claim: An IGH clonotype was defined as a unique nucleotide sequence spanning from the beginning of IGH V gene framework 1 to the 5' end of the C segment.
source: An IGH clonotype was defined as a unique nucleotide sequence spanning from the beginning of IGH V gene framework 1 to the 5' end of the C segment, sufficient to determine isotype.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines what constitutes an IGH clonotype in this study.

claim: The median number of clonotypes was 20,072 per 5×10^4 memory B cells.
source: The median number of clonotypes was 20,072 (14,572–32,806, n=14) per 5×104 memory B cells, 628 (528–981, n=8) per 1×103 plasmablasts, and 800 (623–1183, n=9) per 1×103 plasma cells.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on clonotype numbers per cell subset.

claim: The median number of clonotypes was 628 per 1×10^3 plasmablasts.
source: The median number of clonotypes was 20,072 (14,572–32,806, n=14) per 5×104 memory B cells, 628 (528–981, n=8) per 1×103 plasmablasts, and 800 (623–1183, n=9) per 1×103 plasma cells.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on clonotype numbers per cell subset.

claim: The median number of clonotypes was 800 per 1×10^3 plasma cells.
source: The median number of clonotypes was 20,072 (14,572–32,806, n=14) per 5×104 memory B cells, 628 (528–981, n=8) per 1×103 plasmablasts, and 800 (623–1183, n=9) per 1×103 plasma cells.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on clonotype numbers per cell subset.

claim: Rarefaction analysis in the Bmem subpopulation revealed an asymptotic increase of species richness that did not reach a plateau.
source: Rarefaction analysis in the Bmem subpopulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, left) revealed an asymptotic increase of species richness that did not reach a plateau, indicating that the averaged species richness can only serve as a lower limit of sample diversity estimation.
evidence: The manuscript describes rarefaction analysis results and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For all samples of PBL and PL subpopulations, species richness curves plateaued.
source: For all samples of PBL and PL subpopulations, species richness curves plateaued, meaning that we had reached sufficient sequencing depth to evaluate the clonal diversity of the sorted cell samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, center and right).
evidence: The manuscript describes rarefaction analysis results for PBL and PL subpopulations.

claim: IgM represented more than half of the repertoire in memory B cells.
source: IgM represented more than half of the repertoire in Bmem, while IgA was dominant in PBL and PL (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes isotype distribution in memory B cells with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: IgA was dominant in plasmablasts and plasma cells.
source: IgM represented more than half of the repertoire in Bmem, while IgA was dominant in PBL and PL (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes isotype distribution in ASCs with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: IgG was the second most prevalent isotype in antibody-secreting cells.
source: The second most prevalent isotype in ASCs was IgG, which was also less abundant in Bmem compared to IgA.
evidence: The manuscript describes the relative abundance of IgG in ASCs.

claim: IgD represented a substantial part of the memory B cell clonal repertoire.
source: IgD represented a substantial part of the Bmem clonal repertoire, while <1% clonotypes of ASCs expressed IgD.
evidence: The manuscript describes the proportion of IgD in memory B cells.

claim: Less than 1% of ASC clonotypes expressed IgD.
source: IgD represented a substantial part of the Bmem clonal repertoire, while <1% clonotypes of ASCs expressed IgD.
evidence: The manuscript describes the proportion of IgD in ASCs.

claim: The level of somatic hypermutation was on average significantly higher in ASC subsets compared to memory B cells.
source: The level of SHM was on average significantly higher in ASC subsets, reflecting that PBLs and PLs are enriched for clones that have undergone affinity maturation (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes SHM levels across cell subsets with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Switched isotypes (IgG, IgA) had higher average levels of SHMs in the memory B cell subset compared with IgM and IgD isotypes.
source: The switched isotypes (IgG, IgA) had higher average levels of SHMs in the Bmem subset compared with IgM and IgD isotypes.
evidence: The manuscript describes differences in SHM levels between isotypes in memory B cells.

claim: The SHM level of IgD clonotypes in ASC subsets was significantly higher compared with memory B cells.
source: Interestingly, the SHM level of IgD clonotypes in ASC subsets was significantly higher compared with Bmem.
evidence: The manuscript describes a specific finding about IgD SHM levels in ASCs.

claim: The rate of SHM in plasmablasts was higher than that in plasma cells in clonotypes from IgM, IgA, and IgG isotypes.
source: Of note, the rate of SHM in PBLs was higher than that in PLs in clonotypes from the three most abundant isotypes (i.e., IgM, IgA, and IgG).
evidence: The manuscript describes differences in SHM rates between PBL and PL.

claim: Plasmablasts had significantly longer CDR3 regions compared to memory B cells on average in every isotype except for IgE.
source: PBLs had significantly longer CDR3 regions compared to Bmem cells on average in every isotype except for IgE (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript describes CDR3 length differences with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: IGHV gene segment usage was roughly similar between memory B cells, plasmablasts, and plasma cells from all donors.
source: IGHV gene segment usage was roughly similar between Bmem, PBL, and PL cells from all donors, indicating generally equal probabilities of memory-to-ASC conversion for B cells carrying BCRs encoded by distinct gene segments (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The manuscript describes IGHV gene usage patterns across cell subsets.

claim: IGHV gene segment usage differed significantly between the studied cell subsets and naive B cells.
source: This distribution differed significantly between the studied cell subsets and naive B cells (based on data from Gidoni et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript compares IGHV usage to naive B cells from a cited study.

claim: Statistically significant Pearson correlations in terms of IGHV gene frequencies were observed for all pairs between memory B cells, plasmablasts, or plasma cells (>0.95 correlation, p<0.01).
source: We observed statistically significant Pearson correlations in terms of IGHV gene frequencies for all pairs between Bmem, PBL, or PL (>0.95 correlation, p<0.01), and for naive vs. Btot (0.79 correlation, p<0.01).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical correlation values for IGHV gene frequencies.

claim: Pearson correlation coefficients for the fold-change of IGHV gene segment usage frequencies were 0.95 for memory B cells and plasmablasts, 0.96 for memory B cells and plasma cells, and 0.98 for plasmablasts and plasma cells (p<0.01 for all pairs).
source: Pearson correlation coefficients for the fold-change of IGHV gene segment usage frequencies were 0.95 for Bmem and PBL, 0.96 for Bmem and PL, and 0.98 for PBL and PL (p<0.01 for all pairs).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical correlation values for IGHV gene segment fold-changes.

claim: IGHV gene segment under- or overrepresentation clearly depended on the given gene sequence.
source: Moreover, IGHV gene segment under- or overrepresentation clearly depended on the given gene sequence.
evidence: The manuscript describes a pattern in IGHV gene representation.

claim: Most IGHV segments in each of the four major clusters behaved concordantly with other segments in that cluster.
source: We clustered IGHV genes based on their sequence similarity, and observed that most IGHV segments in each of the four major clusters behaved concordantly with other segments in that cluster (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript describes clustering analysis results with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: IGH repertoires of memory B cells, plasmablasts, and plasma cells subsets are private to a large degree.
source: Both metrics showed significantly higher inter-individual differences compared to the divergence of repertoires derived from the same donor, reflecting the fact that IGH repertoires of Bmem, PBL, and PL subsets are private to a large degree (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The manuscript describes repertoire similarity analysis with reference to Figure 2A and B.

claim: Identical clonotypes were observed in the repertoires of plasmablasts and plasma cells collected at different time points.
source: We observed identical clonotypes in the repertoires of PBL and PL collected at different time points, whereas the repertoire similarity was much lower compared to that between replicate samples, reflecting the transient nature of PBL and PL populations in peripheral blood.
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal dynamics of ASC repertoires.

claim: Lower clonal overlap was observed in plasmablasts and plasma cells for more distant time points (separated by 11 or 12 months) than those that are closer together (1 month).
source: Notably, we observed lower clonal overlap in PBL and PL for more distant time points (separated by 11 or 12 months) than those that are closer together (1 month) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns in clonal overlap with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The dissimilarity between samples collected on the same day vs. 1 month or even 1 year later was much lower for memory B cells.
source: The dissimilarity between samples collected on the same day vs. 1 month or even 1 year later was much lower for Bmem, demonstrating the high stability of the clonal repertoire and long-term persistence of IGH clonotypes in these cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the stability of memory B cell repertoires over time.

claim: The average number of shared clonotypes in memory B cells was significantly higher between fractions of the most abundant clonotypes compared to randomly sampled clonotypes.
source: Indeed, the average number of shared clonotypes in Bmem was significantly higher between fractions of the most abundant clonotypes compared to randomly sampled clonotypes (Figure 2C), as well as when compared to the most abundant clonotypes shared by two naive repertoires (from Gidoni et al., 2019) or to pre-immune IGH repertoires obtained by in silico generation using OLGA software (Sethna et al., 2019; Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript describes clonotype sharing analysis with reference to Figure 2C and cited studies.

claim: There were no shared clonotypes defined by their full-length nucleotide sequence.
source: We also noted that there were no shared clonotypes defined by their full-length nucleotide sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the absence of full-length nucleotide sequence sharing.

claim: Public clonotypes were hypermutated, although the rate of SHM was slightly lower compared to that in clonotypes specific to one donor (private).
source: Public clonotypes were also hypermutated, although the rate of SHM was slightly lower compared to that in clonotypes specific to one donor (private) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes SHM levels in public vs. private clonotypes.

claim: The extent of clonal overlap was significantly higher between naive repertoires than for in silico-generated repertoires.
source: Of note, the extent of clonal overlap was significantly higher between naive repertoires than for in silico-generated repertoires, indicating functional convergence even in pre-immune repertoires.
evidence: The manuscript compares clonal overlap between naive and in silico repertoires.

claim: Public clonotypes were more likely to be detected than private ones in samples collected at different time points.
source: Finally, we found that public clonotypes were more likely to be detected than private ones in samples collected at different time points (Figure 2E), again suggesting persistent memory to common antigens.
evidence: The manuscript describes persistence patterns of public vs. private clonotypes.

claim: 190 clonal lineages consisting of at least 20 unique clonotypes were identified across the four donors from whom samples were collected at each of the three time points.
source: We focused on larger clonal lineages consisting of at least 20 unique clonotypes from the corresponding donor. On average, these clonal lineages covered 3.4% of a given donor's repertoire, and we identified 190 such lineages across the four donors from whom samples were collected at each of the three time points (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on clonal lineages analyzed.

claim: The clonal lineages were divided into two large clusters using k-means clustering algorithm, based on the proportion of represented cell subsets and BCR isotypes.
source: To investigate the nature of such bimodal distribution and perform comparative analysis of these two types of clonal lineages, we divided them into two large clusters using k-means clustering algorithm, based on the proportion of represented cell subsets and BCR isotypes (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the clustering methodology used.

claim: The HBmem cluster included 138 clonal lineages and was mostly composed of memory B cell clonotypes of non-switched isotype IgM.
source: The more abundant HBmem cluster included 138 clonal lineages, and was mostly composed of Bmem clonotypes of non-switched isotype IgM.
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of the HBmem cluster.

claim: The LBmem cluster included 52 clonal lineages and was more diverse and largely composed of ASCs, and enriched in IgG and IgA clonotypes.
source: Conversely, the smaller LBmem cluster (52 clonal lineages) was more diverse and largely composed of ASCs, and enriched in IgG and IgA clonotypes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of the LBmem cluster.

claim: The average size of clonal lineages did not differ between the HBmem and LBmem clusters.
source: The average size of clonal lineages (i.e., the number of unique clonotypes per lineage) did not differ between the HBmem and LBmem clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), and both clusters were present in repertoires of all donors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the size comparison of clonal lineages between clusters.

claim: HBmem groups were quite stable over time, while LBmem lineages had a burst of increased frequency at one of the time points.
source: The two clusters of lineages demonstrated different temporal behavior; while HBmem groups were quite stable over time, LBmem lineages had a burst of increased frequency at one of the time points (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal dynamics of the two clusters with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Persistence of a clonal lineage was strongly associated with its composition.
source: Persistence of a clonal lineage was strongly associated with its composition (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between persistence and composition.

claim: Clonal lineages enriched with clonotypes or with the IgM isotype were more likely to persist through time.
source: Clonal lineages enriched with clonotypes or with the IgM isotype – including all HBmem lineages – were more likely to persist through time.
evidence: The manuscript describes persistence patterns related to isotype composition.

claim: Lineages with larger proportions of ASCs or IgG/IgA isotypes tended to have lower persistence, with a burst of increased frequency at one particular time point.
source: Conversely, lineages with larger proportions of ASCs or IgG/IgA isotypes, including most LBmem lineages, tended to have lower persistence, with a burst of increased frequency at one particular time point.
evidence: The manuscript describes persistence patterns related to ASC and isotype composition.

claim: The frequencies of clonal lineages were highly correlated among replicate samples.
source: The frequencies of clonal lineages were highly correlated among replicate samples, and the persistence of a clonal lineage was not associated with its size (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F), indicating that differences in persistence cannot be attributed to clonotype sampling noise.
evidence: The manuscript describes the correlation of clonal lineage frequencies in replicates.

claim: The persistence of a clonal lineage was not associated with its size.
source: The frequencies of clonal lineages were highly correlated among replicate samples, and the persistence of a clonal lineage was not associated with its size (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F), indicating that differences in persistence cannot be attributed to clonotype sampling noise.
evidence: The manuscript describes the lack of association between persistence and lineage size.

claim: HBmem lineages were enriched in clonotypes detected at multiple time points.
source: Besides their higher persistence, the HBmem lineages were enriched in clonotypes detected at multiple time points (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G), indicating that persistent clonal lineages are supported by persistent clonotypes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal detection patterns of HBmem clonotypes.

claim: 29.7% of the HBmem cluster was represented by public clonal lineages shared between at least two donors.
source: Furthermore, 29.7% of the HBmem cluster was represented by public clonal lineages shared between at least two donors, compared to 3.8% for the LBmem cluster.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on public clonal lineages in each cluster.

claim: 3.8% of the LBmem cluster was represented by public clonal lineages shared between at least two donors.
source: Furthermore, 29.7% of the HBmem cluster was represented by public clonal lineages shared between at least two donors, compared to 3.8% for the LBmem cluster.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on public clonal lineages in each cluster.

claim: The G-MRCA distance was on average fivefold higher in LBmem clonal lineages compared to HBmem (median = 0.044 vs. 0.008).
source: The G-MRCA distance was on average fivefold higher in LBmem clonal lineages compared to HBmem (median = 0.044 vs. 0.008, Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative comparison of G-MRCA distances between clusters.

claim: In most (38 out of 52) LBmem lineages, some memory B cell clonotypes were observed at the time point preceding expansion.
source: In most (38 out of 52) LBmem lineages, some Bmem clonotypes were observed at the time point preceding expansion.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on memory B cell detection in LBmem lineages.

claim: Clonotypes of LBmem lineages are typically characterized by lower pairwise divergence compared to that in HBmem lineages (median = 0.11 vs. 0.13).
source: Moreover, clonotypes of LBmem lineages are typically characterized by lower pairwise divergence compared to that in HBmem lineages (median = 0.11 vs. 0.13, Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative comparison of pairwise divergence between clusters.

claim: One clear example of a transition from HBmem to LBmem state was found in the evolutionary history of a clonal lineage.
source: We found one clear example of a transition from HBmem to LBmem state in the evolutionary history of a clonal lineage (Figure 4F,I).
evidence: The manuscript describes a specific example with reference to Figure 4F and I.

claim: In both the HBmem and LBmem clonal lineages, a higher ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous SHMs was observed in the G-MRCA branches compared to subsequent tree branches.
source: In both the HBmem and LBmem clonal lineages, we observed a higher ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous SHMs in the G-MRCA branches compared to subsequent tree branches, meaning that a fraction of SHMs acquired by MRCA was further fixed by positive selection.
evidence: The manuscript describes selection patterns in both clusters.

claim: The fraction of SHMs fixed by positive selection was higher in LBmem lineages (Fisher's exact test: α=0.58 and 0.65, p<10–6 and <10–15 in HBmem and LBmem, respectively).
source: However, this fraction was higher in LBmem lineages (Fisher's exact test: α=0.58 and 0.65, p<10–6 and <10–15 in HBmem and LBmem, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results for positive selection.

claim: α of distinct clonal lineages was generally higher in LBmem than in HBmem (median α=0.57 vs. α=0.18).
source: α of distinct clonal lineages was also generally higher in LBmem than in HBmem (median α=0.57 vs. α=0.18, Figure 5B), showing that positive selection more frequently preceded expansion of LBmem than HBmem lineages.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative comparison of α values between clusters.

claim: The πNπS of both clusters was <1.
source: The πNπS of both clusters was <1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on πNπS values.

claim: The πNπS ratio was lower in the LBmem cluster, indicating stronger negative selection.
source: The πNπS ratio was lower in the LBmem cluster, indicating stronger negative selection.
evidence: The manuscript describes the interpretation of πNπS values.

claim: A larger proportion of the LBmem SFS corresponds to high frequencies compared to HBmem.
source: A larger proportion of the LBmem SFS corresponds to high frequencies compared to HBmem (Figure 5D), indicating weaker negative and/or stronger positive selection in LBmem SFS.
evidence: The manuscript describes SFS patterns with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: Normalized πNπS was significantly higher in the high-frequency (>60%) bins of SHMs in LBmem clonal lineages.
source: Normalized πNπS was significantly higher in the high-frequency (>60%) bins of SHMs in LBmem clonal lineages.
evidence: The manuscript describes normalized πNπS patterns in high-frequency bins.

claim: Reactivation of LBmem lineages is coupled with strengthening of both positive selection on the G-MRCA branch and both positive and negative selection during subsequent clonal lineage expansion.
source: We thus observed that reactivation of LBmem lineages is coupled with strengthening of both types of selection: positive on the G-MRCA branch, and both positive and negative during subsequent clonal lineage expansion.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the selection patterns observed in LBmem lineages.

claim: HBmem evolved more neutrally under weaker negative selection, suggesting absence of antigen challenge during the observation period.
source: HBmem, in contrast, evolved more neutrally under weaker negative selection, suggesting absence of antigen challenge during the observation period (Figure 5F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the evolutionary pattern of HBmem lineages.

claim: B cells play a crucial role in protection from various pathogens and cancer cells as well as regulation of the immune response.
source: B cells play a crucial role in protection from various pathogens and cancer cells as well as regulation of the immune response (Akkaya et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this general statement about B cell function.

claim: The structural diversity of B cell receptors is responsible for the B cell-mediated immune system's capacity to recognize a wide variety of different antigens.
source: The structural diversity of B cell receptors (BCRs) is responsible for the B cell-mediated immune system's capacity to recognize a wide variety of different antigens, and every individual harbors a large pool of naive B cell clones, each with a unique BCR.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about BCR diversity.

claim: Antigenic challenge triggers the proliferation and maturation of naive B cells with cognate BCRs.
source: Antigenic challenge triggers the proliferation and maturation of naive B cells with cognate BCRs, and the resulting progeny comprise a number of cell subsets with differing functions and lifespans.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about B cell activation.

claim: During the affinity maturation process, the initial structure of a given BCR can change at the genomic level as a result of somatic hypermutation.
source: During the affinity maturation process, the initial structure of a given BCR can change at the genomic level as a result of somatic hypermutation (SHM), a process that accompanies B cell proliferation after antigen-specific activation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the mechanism of BCR diversification.

claim: Cells bearing BCRs with higher affinity to the antigen are favored during the affinity maturation process.
source: Cells bearing BCRs with higher affinity to the antigen are favored during the affinity maturation process, and produce signals that stimulate further differentiation and expansion (De Silva and Klein, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this statement about affinity maturation.

claim: The five main classes, or isotypes, of antibodies (i.e., IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, and IgM) have different functions in the immune response.
source: The five main classes, or isotypes, of antibodies (i.e., IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, and IgM) have different functions in the immune response (Stavnezer et al., 2008; Vidarsson et al., 2014), and isotype switching during clonal proliferation can thereby change the functional capabilities of B cells and the antibodies they produce.
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this statement about antibody isotypes.

claim: Immune repertoire sequencing techniques provide valuable insights into the development and structure of B cell immunity with clonal-level resolution.
source: Recently developed immune repertoire sequencing techniques provide valuable insights into the development and structure of B cell immunity with clonal-level resolution (Chaudhary and Wesemann, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this statement about sequencing techniques.

claim: Studies of BCR repertoires of patients with different diseases have made an important contribution to the understanding of mechanisms of pathology and B cell-mediated immunity.
source: Studies of BCR repertoires of patients with different diseases have made an important contribution to the understanding of mechanisms of pathology and B cell-mediated immunity (Bashford-Rogers et al., 2019; Nielsen et al., 2020; Gaebler et al., 2021; Sakharkar et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support this statement about disease studies.

claim: Longitudinal analysis of repertoires at different time points has made it possible to study the dynamics of B cell response following antigenic challenge or therapy.
source: Longitudinal analysis of repertoires at different time points has made it possible to study the dynamics of B cell response following antigenic challenge or therapy (Laserson et al., 2014; Davydov et al., 2018; Horns et al., 2019; Nourmohammad et al., 2019; Hoehn et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support this statement about longitudinal studies.

claim: De Bourcy et al. reported on age-related differences in the structure of clonal lineages, somatic hypermutagenesis and affinity maturation processes, and differences in recall response of persisting lineages upon vaccination depending on CMV seropositivity status.
source: De Bourcy et al. recently reported on age-related differences in the structure of clonal lineages, somatic hypermutagenesis and affinity maturation processes, and differences in recall response of persisting lineages upon vaccination depending on CMV seropositivity status (de Bourcy et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific study and its findings.

claim: Studies have described in detail the action of positive selection in the evolution of clonal lineages in vaccination and chronic HIV infection.
source: Other studies have described in detail the action of positive selection in the evolution of clonal lineages in vaccination and chronic HIV infection (Bonsignori et al., 2017; Horns et al., 2019; Nourmohammad et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support this statement about positive selection.

claim: Reports have described persisting clonal lineages which are predominantly represented by cells with IgM/IgD isotypes, and which demonstrate signs of neutral evolution.
source: Reports have also described persisting clonal lineages which are predominantly represented by cells with IgM/IgD isotypes, and which demonstrate signs of neutral evolution (Horns et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this statement about persisting lineages.

claim: Wu et al. observed the clonal stability of plasma cells in bone marrow, representing the largest fraction of ASCs in the human body.
source: Wu et al. observed the clonal stability of plasma cells (PL) in bone marrow (Wu et al., 2010), representing the largest fraction of ASCs in the human body.
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific study and its findings.

claim: Recent studies have described differences in BCR repertoires of IgM and switched memory B cells as well as the complex interplay between CD27high and CD27low B cell memory subsets.
source: For example, recent studies have described differences in BCR repertoires of IgM and switched memory B cells as well as the complex interplay between CD27high and CD27low B cell memory subsets, showing the complex nature of B cell immune memory (Wu et al., 2010; Grimsholm et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this statement about memory B cell subsets.

claim: BCR repertoires of antigen-experienced B cell subsets and their dynamics are usually studied in the context of pathologic conditions and vaccination.
source: BCR repertoires of antigen-experienced B cell subsets and their dynamics are usually studied in the context of pathologic conditions and vaccination, and there is little equivalent data in the absence of acute or chronic immune response.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a gap in the literature.

claim: The study used advanced IgH repertoire profiling technology that provides full-length IgH variable region sequences with isotype annotation.
source: In order to obtain detailed and unbiased repertoire data, we used advanced IgH repertoire profiling technology that provides full-length IgH variable region sequences with isotype annotation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The study cohort consisted of four males and two females aged 23, 27, 27, 33, 33, and 39 years.
source: Blood samples from six (four males and two females) young and middle-aged donors (23, 27, 27, 33, 33, and 39 years of age) without severe inflammatory diseases, chronic or recent acute infectious diseases, or vaccinations were collected at three time points (T1 – 0, T2 – 1 month, T3 – 12 months); donor details and the number cells collected for each time point and cell subset are provided in Table 1.
evidence: The manuscript provides demographic information about the study cohort.

claim: Four donors suffered allergic rhinitis to pollen, and two also suffered from food allergy.
source: Four donors suffered allergic rhinitis to pollen, and two also suffered from food allergy.
evidence: The manuscript provides health status information about the donors.

claim: The study was approved by the Local Ethical Committee of Pirogov Russian National Research Medical University, Moscow, Russia (abstract #190 November 18, 2019).
source: The study was approved by the Local Ethical Committee of Pirogov Russian National Research Medical University, Moscow, Russia (abstract #190 November 18, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript provides ethical approval information.

claim: IGH cDNA libraries were prepared using a rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE) approach with a template-switch effect.
source: IGH cDNA libraries were prepared as described previously (Turchaninova et al., 2016) with several modifications. Briefly, we used a rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE) approach with a template-switch effect to introduce 5' adaptors during cDNA synthesis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the library preparation methodology.

claim: Prepared libraries were sequenced with an Illumina HiSeq 2000/2500 (paired-end, 2×310 bp).
source: Prepared libraries were then sequenced with an Illumina HiSeq 2000/2500 (paired-end, 2×310 bp).
evidence: The manuscript describes the sequencing platform and parameters used.

claim: Sample demultiplexing by sample barcodes and UMI-based error correction were performed using MIGEC v1.2.7 software.
source: Sample demultiplexing by sample barcodes introduced in the 5' adapter and UMI-based error correction were performed using MIGEC v1.2.7 software (Shugay et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript describes the bioinformatics tools used for data processing.

claim: Alignment of sequences, V-, D-, J-, and C-segment annotation, and reconstruction of clonal repertoires were accomplished using MiXCR v3.0.10.
source: Alignment of sequences, V-, D-, J-, and C-segment annotation, and reconstruction of clonal repertoires were accomplished using MiXCR v3.0.10 (Bolotin et al., 2015) with prior removal of the primer-originated component of the C-segment.
evidence: The manuscript describes the bioinformatics tools used for sequence alignment and annotation.

claim: TIgGER software was used to derive an individual database of V gene alleles for each donor.
source: Using TIgGER (Gadala-Maria et al., 2015) software, we derived an individual database of V gene alleles for each donor and realigned all sequences for precise detection of hypermutations.
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of TIgGER for V gene allele determination.

claim: Change-O v0.4.4 was utilized to assign clonal groups, defined as groups of clonotypes with the same V segment, CDR3 length, and at least 85% similarity in CDR3 nucleotide sequence.
source: Change-O v0.4.4 (Gupta et al., 2015) was utilized to assign clonal groups, defined as groups of clonotypes with the same V segment, CDR3 length, and at least 85% similarity in CDR3 nucleotide sequence.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology for clonal group assignment.

claim: Phylogenetic trees were reconstructed with RAxML v8.2.11, using the GTRGAMMA evolutionary model and germline sequence as an outgroup.
source: Next, we reconstructed the clonal lineage's phylogeny with RAxML v8.2.11, using the GTRGAMMA evolutionary model and germline sequence as an outgroup, and computed marginal ancestral states (Stamatakis, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript describes the phylogenetic reconstruction methodology.

claim: The obtained IGH isotype distributions based on unique clonotypes roughly correspond to the distribution of IGH isotypes typically detected by flow cytometry of the same subsets.
source: The obtained IGH isotype distributions based on unique clonotypes roughly correspond to the distribution of IGH isotypes typically detected by flow cytometry of the same subsets (Perez-Andres et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript compares their findings to published flow cytometry data.

claim: Plasmablasts and plasma cells with heavily hypermutated BCRs could be the subset of B cell progeny that continue to acquire mutations after optimal affinity has been achieved.
source: We hypothesize that such PBLs with heavily hypermutated BCRs could be the subset of B cell progeny that continue to acquire mutations after optimal affinity has been achieved, while another part of the clonal progeny is committed to a long-lived PL fate and acquires the CD138 marker characteristic of this cell subset (Garimalla et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript presents a hypothesis based on their observations and cites a reference.

claim: The differences in V usage frequencies between naive and antigen-experienced B cell subsets have been reported in several previous studies.
source: These differences in V usage frequencies between naive and antigen-experienced B cell subsets have also been reported in several previous studies, even though different FACS gating strategies were used (Mitsunaga and Snyder, 2020; Ghraichy et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support the reproducibility of their findings.

claim: Initial recruitment of B cells to the immune response is in many cases determined by the germline-encoded parts of the BCR, presumably CDR1 and CDR2.
source: Our findings further support the idea that initial recruitment of B cells to the immune response is in many cases determined by the germline-encoded parts of the BCR, presumably CDR1 and CDR2.
evidence: The manuscript presents an interpretation of their findings.

claim: Previous studies have shown high levels of convergence in IGHV usage between B cell clonotypes specific for particular pathogens or self-antigens.
source: Previous studies have shown high levels of convergence in IGHV usage between B cell clonotypes specific for particular pathogens or self-antigens (Peng et al., 2019; Galson et al., 2015; Bashford-Rogers et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this statement about IGHV convergence.

claim: The finding of memory B cell subset stability expands the recent observation of Bmem subset stability in elderly donors on a larger cohort of donors of younger age.
source: Our finding expands the recent observation of Bmem subset stability in elderly donors (Phad et al., 2022) on a larger cohort of donors of younger age.
evidence: The manuscript compares their findings to a recent study.

claim: Two recent studies on extra-deep repertoires of bulk peripheral blood B cells reported 1–6% or ~1% shared V-CDR3aa-J clonotypes between pairs of unrelated donors.
source: Two recent studies on extra-deep repertoires of bulk peripheral blood B cells reported 1–6% (Soto et al., 2019) or ~1% (Briney et al., 2019) shared V-CDR3aa-J clonotypes between pairs of unrelated donors, with lower repertoire convergence for class-switched clonotypes shown in the latter study.
evidence: The manuscript cites references to compare their findings to previous studies.

claim: Using the same method as Briney et al., the study measured 0.06% repertoire overlap in the Bmem subset.
source: Using the same method, we similarly measured 0.06% repertoire overlap in the Bmem subset (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript provides a quantitative comparison to a previous study.

claim: The model proposed by Briney et al. suggests that IGH repertoires are initially dissimilar and then homogenize during B cell development before finally becoming highly individualized after immunological exposure.
source: Complementing the model proposed by Briney et al. – wherein IGH repertoires are initially dissimilar and then homogenize during B cell development before finally becoming highly individualized after immunological exposure – we found a significantly higher number of shared clonotypes between IGH repertoires among the most abundant Bmem clonotypes, indicating functional convergence presumably due to exposure to common environmental antigens.
evidence: The manuscript describes a model from a cited study and how their findings complement it.

claim: Horns and colleagues observed lineages with very similar features to HBmem, which also possessed persistent dynamics against a background of vaccine-responsive lineages and were predominantly composed of the IgM isotype.
source: Horns and colleagues observed lineages with very similar features to HBmem, which also possessed persistent dynamics against a background of vaccine-responsive lineages and were predominantly composed of the IgM isotype (Horns et al., 2019).
